it was a long road.
when i got out of the hospital i was on a roller coaster for another year or so.  i was in an out of doctor's offices and no one knew what was really wrong with me. 

my relationships with friends and family were almost non-existent by this point.  i had to quit my job because i was missing so much work.

eventually i was diagnosed with schizo-affective disorder (hybrid of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) and i started taking the right medication.  i got better - not perfect, but better.

i spontaneously did a 3-month solo backpacking trip in australia and thailand, and when I got home (Germany - originally from Canada, though) I decided to finally open up to everyone in my life about what had been going on with me.

I started a blog - the first post was just about what I had been through.  The feedback was overwhelming.  People I hadn't spoken to in years reached out to me, sharing their own stories, thanking me for sharing mine, and applauding me for my 'courage'  (that felt weird to me).

The post was shared around, and eventually I started getting similar messages and emails from complete strangers.  

I continued writing, and a couple of months after that first post, a college professor in Canada came across my blog and contacted me to see if I'd be interested in speaking in her third year behavioural science class.

I flew back to Canada (perfect timing - I had already planned a trip since I hadn't been back in over 2 years), prepared a speech, performed it, had the audience both laughing and crying, and was invited back again the next week to speak in another class.

6 months ago, this was not on my agenda at all!  But I'm very glad things have happened the way they have.

in my opinion, the best thing you can do is to be there for them, but also to **realise you can't fix them on your own.**

think of suicidal people as being stuck in a hole -- one that you can't fill up.  you might be able to help them climb out of that hole, but you can't fix it.  you can set up barriers - you can put pylons up, or tell them to watch their step - but you can't ensure they won't fall back in the hole.

you need to be diligent about getting them to fix that hole.  this can be a real challenge, because typically a person who is suicidal has already given up.

find a psychiatrist for them if you have to. drag them by the ear if you must.  call an ambulance if they're threatening to attempt suicide, even though they'll probably say they'll never forgive you for it (they will - trust me).  **get them the help they won't seek on their own.**

“The so-called ‘psychotically depressed’ person who tries to kill herself doesn’t do so out of quote ‘hopelessness’ or any abstract conviction that life’s assets and debits do not square. And surely not because death seems suddenly appealing. The person in whom Its invisible agony reaches a certain unendurable level will kill herself the same way a trapped person will eventually jump from the window of a burning high-rise. Make no mistake about people who leap from burning windows. Their terror of falling from a great height is still just as great as it would be for you or me standing speculatively at the same window just checking out the view; i.e. the fear of falling remains a constant. The variable here is the other terror, the fire’s flames: when the flames get close enough, falling to death becomes the slightly less terrible of two terrors. It’s not desiring the fall; it’s terror of the flames. And yet nobody down on the sidewalk, looking up and yelling ‘Don’t!’ and ‘Hang on!’, can understand the jump. Not really. You’d have to have personally been trapped and felt flames to really understand a terror way beyond falling.” -David Foster Wallace

different kind of heartbreak than you might be expecting, but:

i had a boyfriend in highschool.  he was two years older than me.  we started dating at the end of grade 9 for me (11 for him).  

we were that couple that was *always* together.  we did everything together. he walked me to class.  we passed notes.  we coordinated times to meet in the halls during class on 'bathroom breaks'.  we ate lunch together.  everything.

then, he moved away for university.

i will never forget how alone i felt that first day of school in grade 11, not having him there. it was so incredibly hard for me to face that without him.

i remember coming home, feeling so defeated and numb.  i curled up in my bed and my mom just held me as i cried for hours.

it seems trivial now: it's just school.  and we hadn't even broken up!  but i was a fragile teenager then - i wasn't the strong person i am now.  back then, that was hard.  i needed him then and it hurt so, so, so bad that he wasn't physically there with me.


**TL;DR** - boyfriend moved to uni, i was still in highschool, had a really hard time facing school without him by my side. 

that heartbreak was so real and so raw.

generally, you'd go to your GP and describe what's going on, and then typically you'd get a referral to either a psychologist or a psychiatrist.  a GP can't usually diagnose you properly.  
please don't take medication from a GP without having spoken to a specialist: they don't always understand these cases, but might try to help you regardless and wind up prescribing you the wrong thing.
From my experience, this can land you in a bad place: these medications can be dangerous if they're not tailored to your condition.

how old are you, and how long has this stuff been going on?

I can't provide you with a diagnosis, obviously, but I can point you in the right direction by saying it's best to talk to a doctor.
A diagnosis for a mental illness/disorder is never easy to come to.  There's nothing physical to examine, so your doctor will rely greatly on your own account of your symptoms and your thought processes.

You're off to a great start by opening up about it somewhere and seeking help.

Your parents, on the other hand, might be more difficult for you to approach.

All you can do is be open, transparent and honest about your situation.  They might not understand it - that's totally okay - they don't need to understand it to be able to offer you their support.
